messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Kelepi sits stiffly in the chair, his large hands resting on his knees, palms down. For the last six months, a fog has settled over his life, a haze he traces back to a single, searingly clear moment. He had been driving his wife, Leilani, home from a celebratory dinner. The headlights came out of nowhere, a sudden glare on the wet road, followed by the sickening shriek of metal. When he came to, the car was silent except for the rhythmic ticking of the hazard lights and the sound of rain on the shattered windshield. He turned to Leilani. He remembers her hand, resting limp and unnaturally bent on the dashboard, the silver of her wedding ring stark against the blood. That image is burned into his mind. In his memory, he can still hear the low, rasping sound of her breathing, a sound that stopped before the paramedics arrived.

In the weeks that followed, Kelepi found he couldn't speak about it. When his in-laws asked for details, the words would catch in his throat. He would start, describing the rain or the dinner they’d just had, but as he neared the moment of impact, the sequence would shatter. The thread of the story would vanish, leaving him staring into space, lost and unable to finish. The memory itself, when it came unbidden, was a sensory assault. It wasn't a narrative but a collection of fragments: the sound of the collision replaying in his ears, the overwhelming wave of grief that felt like drowning, and always, the image of her hand. He began to believe that his inability to save her, to do anything but sit there frozen, was a fundamental stain on his character. He was a weak man; a real man would have protected his wife. This thought became a constant, quiet companion.

His work as a nanny for the Miller family, once a source of joy, became a minefield. He cares for two young children, and their simple, daily existence is now fraught with triggers. Last week, seven-year-old Maya fell off her scooter in the park. Kelepi rushed to her side, and as he reached for her, he saw her small, scraped hand, the skin broken. The sight was a gut punch. The playground faded, replaced by the smell of rain and gasoline. He heard the faint, high-pitched whine of a siren in his head. He felt a paralyzing coldness spread through his limbs, the same helplessness he’d felt in the wrecked car. He could only stare at Maya’s hand, unable to speak or comfort her. It was Maya’s crying that finally broke the spell, but the damage was done. Mrs. Miller later expressed her concern about his "detachment."

Kelepi understands her concern. He feels detached himself, as if he is merely a function, an object designed to perform childcare tasks. He goes through the motions of making lunches, reading stories, and pushing swings, but feels no connection to it, or to the children he once adored. He feels like a shell, hollowed out by his failure. This sense of being a thing, not a person, has made him retreat even further. When other parents at the park chat about their lives, he finds excuses to walk away. Any mention of loss, even a story on the news about a faraway tragedy, sends a jolt of panic through him. He is certain that his own profound failure is written all over his face for them to see. After the incident with Maya, the Millers gently suggested he take some time off. The thought of losing the one structured part of his life, the one thing keeping him from completely dissolving, was what finally propelled him to seek help. He is terrified of telling his story, of having his weakness confirmed, but the alternative—this empty, silent existence as a ghost in his own life—has become even more frightening.
